young.html: Erwin Schrödinger was a physicist, one of the people who worked out the strange rules of atoms. In 1943, in Dublin, he gave some talks for the public that asked a question from a different science: what is life? How can the rules of physics explain a growing, breathing, living thing?

One of his puzzles was about genes, the instructions passed from parents to children. Genes are tiny, far too small to see. Yet they are copied again and again, for hundreds of years, almost without mistakes. A family’s nose or chin can show up generation after generation. How can something so small stay so steady?

Schrödinger guessed that a gene is one big, carefully built molecule, a kind of code, like Morse code with its dots and dashes. Just a few kinds of symbols, put in a long row, can spell out a huge number of different messages. Ten years later, scientists found that genes are written in the DNA molecule, using a code of four chemical “letters.”

Code builder. Using only two signs, a dot and a dash, how many different codes can you make with 1 sign? (2: · and –.) With 2 signs? (4: ··, ·–, –·, ––.) With 3? With 4? Add them all up. Schrödinger used this very example: with groups of up to four signs you already have enough codes for the whole alphabet. DNA has four letters instead of two. How many codes of 3 letters could it make? (4 × 4 × 4 = 64.)

He also noticed that living things keep themselves in good order while the world around them tends to run down and get messy, the way a tidy room gets messy unless someone keeps tidying. Living things do their tidying by taking in food and sunlight.

full.html: Erwin Schrödinger (1887–1961), born in Vienna, created the wave equation of quantum mechanics in 1926 and shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1933. He left Germany that year, after the Nazis came to power, and in 1939 settled in Dublin at the new Institute for Advanced Studies. In February 1943 he gave three public lectures at Trinity College, Dublin; the book What Is Life? The Physical Aspect of the Living Cell (Cambridge University Press, 1944) came from them.
This book was first published in 1944, so it is still under copyright, and this rung quotes none of it. Everything here is our own summary.

full.text: Question 1: why are atoms so small?

full.html: Turn the question around, Schrödinger says: why are we so big compared with atoms? Because the exact laws of physics and chemistry are statistical: they describe the average behavior of enormous numbers of molecules. If you count $n$ molecules doing something at random, the count is typically off by about $\sqrt n$, so the error is a share of about $1/\sqrt n$. With a hundred molecules that is 10%; with a million, 0.1%. An organism must be built of vast numbers of atoms for its workings to be reliable. This is his “$\sqrt n$ law.”

full.name: gb-root-n
full.cap: Each dot is one trial: n molecules wander at random between the two halves of a box. With 100 molecules the share on the left varies a lot; with a million it barely moves from 50%.

full.title: The √n law
full.q: In a gas, you count the molecules in a small region where you expect 1,000,000. About how far off might the count be, and what percentage is that?

full.text: Question 2: how can a tiny gene be so steady?

full.html: Here is the puzzle. Experiments with X-rays on fruit flies suggested a gene holds at most a million or so atoms, and perhaps far fewer. By the $\sqrt n$ law, anything that small should be shaky and unreliable. Yet genes are copied faithfully over many generations, and the famous lower lip of the Habsburg royal family appeared in portraits across centuries.

Schrödinger’s answer, built on the work of the young physicist Max Delbrück and his colleagues, was quantum mechanics. A gene must be a molecule, held together by the same quantum forces that make molecules stable. To change it you must lift it over an energy barrier, which at body temperature happens only rarely. Those rare jumps are mutations: sudden, lasting changes, just as the geneticists had found.

full.text: The code-script and the aperiodic crystal

full.html: What kind of molecule could hold the plan of a whole organism? Not an ordinary crystal, which repeats the same unit over and over and so says very little. Schrödinger proposed an aperiodic crystal: a solid, orderly structure in which the units do not simply repeat, so that their sequence can carry a message, a code-script. A small number of kinds of unit, in a long enough row, can spell an astronomical number of different plans.

full.title: How much can a code say?
full.q: Schrödinger illustrated the code idea with Morse code’s two signs. How many different groups of 1, 2, 3 or 4 signs can be made? And how many three-letter “words” can DNA’s four letters make?
steps: With two signs: groups of 1, 2, 3 and 4 give $2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 30$ codes.
With four letters, three at a time: $4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$.
The genetic code found in the 1960s uses exactly such three-letter words (codons) for its 20 amino acids.

full.text: Question 3: how does life keep its order?

full.html: The second law of thermodynamics says that the disorder (entropy) of an isolated system tends to grow. A living thing keeps itself highly ordered. It does not break the law, Schrödinger says: it takes order in from outside, from the food it eats (and, in the end, from sunlight), and gives disorder back as heat and waste. He described this as feeding on “negative entropy”; in a later note he agreed that physicists would rather say “free energy.” Life, he concluded, works by producing order from order, guided by the gene’s code, rather than order from the random jostling of molecules.

Three of Schrödinger’s ideas: the laws of large bodies are statistical ($\sqrt n$); the gene must be a stable molecule carrying a code-script; and life keeps its order by taking order from its surroundings.
Thinking living things break the second law of thermodynamics. They are not isolated: the total disorder of a living thing plus its surroundings still grows.

The book’s influence was enormous. Francis Crick, James Watson and Maurice Wilkins, who shared the Nobel Prize for the double helix of DNA (1953), each said that reading it helped turn them toward the problem of the gene. Its main guess came true: genes are long molecules whose sequence of four bases is a code. Biologists have also pointed out what it missed or got wrong: Schrödinger thought the gene was probably a protein, knew nothing of DNA’s role (shown in 1944 by Avery, MacLeod and McCarty), and some of what he said had been said before by geneticists. Even so, it is remembered as the book that invited physicists into biology. In a short epilogue Schrödinger gave his own personal, philosophical view of free will and the self; this rung leaves that to readers.

items: Lucretius, earlier on this ladder, explained life by the motions of atoms. Schrödinger asks why life needs so many of them.
Harvey and Aristotle asked how an egg becomes an animal; Schrödinger’s code-script is a modern answer to “where is the plan?” Waddington, the last science rung, takes the question further.
Dobzhansky described genes in populations; Schrödinger asked what a single gene is made of.
Planck, Bohr and Heisenberg made the quantum physics that Schrödinger used to explain why genes are stable.
Can life be explained entirely by physics and chemistry, or does it need new laws as well?
How can a guess that turns out partly wrong still lead to a great discovery?
What does it mean for a molecule to carry a message?

questions: Why does a family trait, like a dimple, sometimes show up again and again over generations?
A tidy room gets messy by itself, but never tidies itself. How do living things stay “tidy”?
Schrödinger was a physicist writing about biology. What good can come from someone looking at a subject from outside?
With just four letters, DNA spells out every living thing. What other codes do you know that use only a few symbols?
Is it all right to publish a guess? What should a writer say when he isn’t sure?
